title: Primary Flight Controls and Trim Systems

questions.text: A pilot initiates a right bank by applying right aileron input. The aircraft yaws LEFT momentarily despite the intended right turn. What aerodynamic phenomenon causes this, and what is the correct coordinator input?

options.label: A
options.text: Gyroscopic precession — when the right aileron moves down, it acts as a gyroscopic force on the propeller disk, precessing the nose left as a 90-degree reaction; the correct response is to reduce power, which reduces gyroscopic effect and allows the turn to proceed without yaw

options.label: B
options.text: Adverse yaw — the down-deflected right aileron increases lift AND drag on the right wing; the increased drag on the right wing yaws the nose left toward the lowered wing (which is the left wing in a right roll initiation); correct with right rudder simultaneously with right aileron input to coordinate the turn

options.label: C
options.text: P-factor — in a right bank, the propeller disk tilts and the descending blade moves through denser air on the left side, producing more thrust on the left and yawing the nose right; this is incorrectly perceived as a left yaw due to the pilot's vestibular illusion; no corrective input is required

options.label: D
options.text: Spiraling slipstream — the clockwise rotating propeller wash strikes the right side of the vertical fin during a right bank, pushing the nose left; the correct response is left rudder to counteract the slipstream-induced yaw during right turns

questions.explanation: Adverse yaw is the direct result of differential drag from differential aileron deflection. In a right bank initiation: the right aileron deflects DOWN (increasing camber on the right wing) → right wing generates MORE LIFT (good — it rises) but ALSO more PROFILE DRAG. The left aileron deflects UP (decreasing camber on the left wing) → left wing generates less lift (good — it drops) but less drag. The dragging right wing pulls the nose LEFT — adverse to the intended right turn direction. This is why coordinated flight requires simultaneous rudder with aileron: right aileron → right rudder to counteract adverse yaw and keep the slip-skid indicator ball centered. Option A incorrectly identifies gyroscopic precession as the cause — precession is caused by pitch changes acting on the spinning propeller disk, not by aileron deflection. Option D also incorrectly attributes the yaw to spiraling slipstream — the slipstream acts on the vertical fin with approximately constant force regardless of aileron position.

questions.text: A student pilot establishes cruise flight at 3,500 feet, then immediately applies nose-up elevator trim until the yoke pressure is zero. The student then releases the yoke to test the trim setting. The nose immediately pitches up. What error occurred?

options.label: A
options.text: The trim was applied in the correct direction (nose up) but the aircraft is slightly too fast for the trim setting; the pilot should reduce power by 100 RPM and recheck the trim; power and trim interact and must be adjusted together for stable hands-off cruise

options.label: B
options.text: The student applied trim BEFORE establishing and stabilizing the desired cruise attitude with primary controls; trim is designed to relieve pressure from an ALREADY-ESTABLISHED attitude, not to set the attitude independently; the correct technique is to (1) establish the desired attitude and power setting, (2) stabilize, then (3) trim until pressure is relieved; trimming first creates a new, different attitude when controls are released

options.label: C
options.text: The elevator trim is rigged backwards — nose-up trim should result in a nose-down tendency when yoke is released; the maintenance technician should be informed of the reversed trim rigging before the aircraft is flown again

options.label: D
options.text: No error occurred — the nose-up pitch after releasing the yoke is the expected response to any trim adjustment; the trim will stabilize within 30-45 seconds as the phugoid oscillation damps; the student should wait for the self-correcting dynamic stability of the aircraft to return the nose to the trimmed attitude

questions.explanation: This question captures the single most common trim technique error in student pilots: using trim to SET attitude instead of HOLD attitude. The correct sequence is: (1) Establish the desired cruise power setting. (2) Establish the desired pitch attitude with primary controls (yoke/stick). (3) Hold that attitude steady until stabilized. (4) Apply trim until the control pressure is zero — NOT until the aircraft does something different. In this scenario, the student applied nose-up trim while at an unspecified, unstabilized attitude. The trim moved the elevator to a position that holds a nose-up attitude — when the student released the yoke, the trim was holding the elevator at nose-up deflection relative to the original cruise position, causing the pitch-up. The trim hasn't reached the natural equilibrium for the desired cruise attitude because the desired attitude was never established first. Option D mentions phugoid oscillation — this is a real phenomenon (long-period pitch oscillation), but it is not an excuse for incorrect trim technique; the initial pitch-up confirms execution error, not a self-correcting system.

questions.text: During the pre-takeoff runup and control check, the pilot moves the yoke full left and notes that the left aileron rises and the right aileron drops — opposite to expected. The aircraft was recently returned from maintenance. What is the most likely explanation and correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: This is normal — when the yoke is pushed LEFT, the right aileron drops to initiate a left bank by generating more lift on the right wing; the description in the question describes normal aileron function and no corrective action is required; proceed with the takeoff

options.label: B
options.text: The ailerons may be rigged backwards following maintenance — the correct response to left yoke input is left aileron UP (reducing lift on left wing) and right aileron DOWN (increasing lift on right wing) to roll LEFT; if the left aileron RISES and the right aileron DROPS, that is the CORRECT description of left yoke input effects; this is not reversed; the pilot should double-check the visual reference (looking at which aileron from which direction)

options.label: C
options.text: The ailerons were rigged in REVERSE during maintenance — left yoke should cause the LEFT aileron to move DOWN and the RIGHT aileron to move UP; with left yoke producing inverted results (left aileron up, right aileron down instead), any left roll input will actually roll the aircraft RIGHT; aircraft control is reversed; do NOT taxi or take off; contact maintenance immediately

options.label: D
options.text: The right aileron dropping when the yoke is moved left is normal functioning; the left aileron rising confirms the left wing will drop — which is reversed from a left bank; the pilot should perform a precautionary taxi-back and contact maintenance to verify rigging

questions.explanation: This question requires precise aerodynamic knowledge to resolve apparent confusion in the description. Correct aileron behavior on LEFT yoke input: LEFT aileron: deflects UP (reduces camber → less lift → left wing drops). RIGHT aileron: deflects DOWN (increases camber → more lift → right wing rises, left wing lower = LEFT BANK. The description in the question says: 'left aileron RISES, right aileron DROPS' — this IS the correct behavior for left yoke. 'Rises' = up deflection. 'Drops' = down deflection. The student who inverts the visual description (confusing 'rising' with more lift) will incorrectly flag normal function as reversed rigging. Option B correctly identifies that the described behavior is NORMAL. Option C would be the correct answer IF the description truly described reversed ailerons (left aileron going DOWN / right going UP on left input) — but the description as written is actually correct. This is a deliberate high-fidelity trap testing whether the applicant truly understands which aileron goes which direction and WHY.

questions.text: In a full-power climb at Vy in a single-engine piston aircraft, why does the aircraft require continuous right rudder to maintain coordinated (ball-centered) flight?

options.label: A
options.text: The right fuel tank is usually heavier during initial climb due to fuel draw from the left tank first; the asymmetric fuel weight creates a right-roll tendency that requires right rudder to counteract; once both tanks equalize, right rudder pressure decreases

options.label: B
options.text: Four propeller-driven aerodynamic effects all combine to yaw or roll the aircraft LEFT during a full-power high-angle-of-attack climb: (1) P-factor: descending right prop blade in denser air produces more thrust on right side → left yaw; (2) Torque: engine/prop rotate clockwise → aircraft tends to roll left → left yaw; (3) Spiraling slipstream: prop wash strikes LEFT side of vertical tail → left yaw; (4) Gyroscopic precession: pitch-up attitude change on rotating gyroscope → left yaw. All four act simultaneously in full-power climb → sustained right rudder required

options.label: C
options.text: Right rudder is required because the elevator is trimmed nose-up for the climb; the nose-up trim tab deflects airflow rightward across the vertical fin; the rightward airflow creates a left yawing moment on the fuselage that must be countered with right rudder input

options.label: D
options.text: Right rudder is not typically required in Vy climbs in modern aircraft; certified aircraft require that trimmed flight at any normal operating airspeed be achievable without continuous directional input; if right rudder is required in a Vy climb, the aircraft rudder trim should be adjusted to eliminate the need for pilot input

questions.explanation: Four independent aerodynamic phenomena each independently produce a left-yawing or left-rolling tendency during full-power, high-angle-of-attack flight: (1) P-FACTOR: the descending propeller blade (right side, viewed from behind) sweeps through denser air at high AoA, generating more thrust on the right — net yaw: LEFT. (2) TORQUE: the engine and propeller rotate clockwise (from pilot's view, looking forward). Newton's 3rd Law: the aircraft tends to rotate COUNTER-clockwise (left) in reaction — net roll/yaw: LEFT. (3) SPIRALING SLIPSTREAM: the clockwise helix of propwash strikes the left side of the vertical stabilizer at a slight sideways angle — net yaw: LEFT. (4) GYROSCOPIC PRECESSION: when the nose pitches up (as in a climb initiation), the rotating propeller disk (acting as a gyroscope) applies a precessive force 90° ahead in the direction of rotation — for a nose-up pitch change, this produces a LEFT yaw. All four simultaneously push the nose LEFT in a full-power climb — requiring sustained right rudder to maintain coordinated ball-centered flight. Option D is incorrect — published POH procedures do require right rudder in full-power climbs for most single-engine piston aircraft; this is not an airworthiness defect, it is expected behavior.

questions.text: During preflight, a pilot discovers that the right aileron has approximately 20% less upward deflection than the left aileron, likely from a bent pusher rod noted in the maintenance log as 'deferred — non-critical.' May the pilot conduct the flight under 14 CFR 91.7?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — minor asymmetries in control deflection are within the standard airworthiness tolerance; a 20% reduction in right aileron upward travel requires slightly more aileron input but does not constitute an unairworthy condition; the aircraft may be flown with the pilot noting the reduced deflection in their personal logbook

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — if the maintenance log deferred the item as non-critical, an A&P mechanic has already determined the aircraft is airworthy to fly; the PIC may rely on a certificated A&P's airworthiness determination when a maintenance item is officially deferred in the aircraft log

options.label: C
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.7(a) requires the PIC to determine the aircraft is airworthy before each flight; asymmetric aileron deflection affecting roll control authority is a control surface limitation that makes the aircraft unairworthy; a deferral notation in a maintenance log by an A&P does not automatically make the aircraft airworthy for flight; the PIC is legally responsible for the airworthiness determination and must not fly with a known control surface deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — but only for VFR day operations below 3,000 feet AGL where full aileron deflection is not operationally required; 14 CFR 91.7's airworthiness requirement applies to all flight phases, but the FAA's risk-based framework allows PICs to accept minor control limitations for low-risk, short-duration flights

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.7(a) places the airworthiness determination squarely on the PIC: 'The pilot in command of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight.' A 20% asymmetry in primary control deflection — specifically aileron upward travel — affects roll control authority and creates asymmetric control response. This is not a minor cosmetic defect. The implications: (1) In crosswind landing scenarios, the reduced right aileron deflection may prevent adequate bank correction especially in gusty conditions. (2) In full-deflection scenarios (wake turbulence, upset recovery), asymmetric limits reduce control efficacy on one side. (3) The maintenance log 'deferral as non-critical' by an A&P does not constitute an FAA-approved minimum equipment list (MEL) authorization for Part 91 general aviation operations. Most Part 91 light aircraft do not operate with an approved MEL — there is no mechanism for deferring a primary control limitation as airworthy. The PIC who flies with this deficiency bears full legal responsibility. Options A and D invent airworthiness tolerance provisions that do not exist for primary control surfaces. Option B incorrectly extends A&P deferral authority beyond its legal scope.

questions.text: A pilot conducts a preflight inspection and notices the external gust lock has been installed on the control surfaces. The pilot removes it from the external aileron lock pin but cannot find the elevator gust lock key. The pilot contacts the ramp agent, who says 'the key is with the mechanic — he'll be back in 30 minutes.' The pilot decides to depart because 'the elevator moves somewhat — the lock must not be fully engaged.' What is wrong with this decision?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing significant — gust locks typically engage only about 70% of maximum deflection range; if the elevator moves somewhat, the partial range is adequate for normal flight operations; the gust lock key is a maintenance item that can be retrieved after landing

options.label: B
options.text: Critical error — departing with any gust lock in place, even partially engaged, is a catastrophic risk; a gust lock on the elevator that limits deflection will prevent proper rotation and pitch control during takeoff and climb; multiple fatal accidents have occurred from gust locks left in place; the pilot must wait for the key, fully remove the lock, and verify full free range of elevator motion before any flight operation

options.label: C
options.text: Minor concern only — the pilot should perform a full-deflection elevator check during the takeoff roll; if full elevator authority is felt before rotation speed, the lock is confirmed absent; this in-motion check provides the same airworthiness verification as a static preflight check

options.label: D
options.text: The decision is acceptable since the pilot already removed one gust lock; the remaining elevator lock is a maintenance documentation issue that should be logged but does not require grounding the aircraft; the pilot should note it in the maintenance log after landing

questions.explanation: Gust locks left in place are one of the most documented categories of fatal takeoff accident in NTSB records. The NTSB Safety Alert SA-078 specifically addresses this: gust lock accidents account for multiple fatal accidents each year, typically because the aircraft appears to taxi and takeoff normally until rotation — at which point full back elevator is unavailable, the aircraft either cannot rotate or rotates to a limited pitch attitude, and cannot clear obstacles or maintain climb. The phrase 'the elevator moves somewhat' is the deadliest rationalization in this scenario: gust locks often allow partial movement but prevent the full deflection needed for rotation and climb control. An elevator with even 30% restricted upward deflection may be unable to rotate a loaded aircraft. Options: WAIT for the key. Remove the lock fully. Verify FULL AND FREE elevator motion — floor to ceiling, full back pressure confirmed. Then and only then, proceed. Option C invents the 'in-motion check' as a substitute for preflight — the takeoff roll is not the time to discover elevator restriction. Option D normalizes flying with a gust lock as a 'maintenance documentation issue.'

questions.text: A low-hour student pilot is practicing steep turns to the left. The student applies left aileron, looks at the bank angle, and notices the nose is yawing RIGHT — opposite to the expected turn direction in the initial bank setup. The student is confused and thinks: 'The rudder is doing something wrong — I should add MORE left aileron to force the bank faster.' What is the correct interpretation and action?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct — the right yaw during left bank initiation indicates the rudder system is malfunctioning; more left aileron will correct the yaw by increasing the lift differential between wings, which has more authority than the errant rudder; the student should press left aileron to full deflection

options.label: B
options.text: The right yaw is ADVERSE YAW — the expected aerodynamic effect of initiating a left bank with ailerons; the down-left aileron generates more drag on the left wing, pulling the nose right; it is not a malfunction; the correct action is to add LEFT RUDDER simultaneously with the left aileron input to counteract adverse yaw and coordinate the turn; adding more aileron without added rudder will worsen the uncoordinated condition

options.label: C
options.text: The right yaw indicates a left crosswind — the aircraft is weathervaning into a left wind; the student should recognize that steep turns in crosswind conditions require opposite rudder to prevent weathervaning; add right rudder to compensate for the crosswind and then roll into the steep left turn without left rudder

options.label: D
options.text: The right yaw during left turn initiation is normal and self-correcting — once the bank is established at 45 degrees, the aerodynamic forces balance and the yaw neutralizes; no rudder input is required; student pilots should avoid using rudder in steep turns because it makes the ball difficult to manage

questions.explanation: This question combines adverse yaw knowledge with the practical application of coordination. The student's misinterpretation ('the rudder is doing something wrong') represents a lack of understanding that the right yaw during left bank initiation is expected and normal — it is adverse yaw, not a malfunction. The student's proposed solution (more left aileron) would actually worsen the situation: more left aileron → more down-deflection of left aileron → even more drag on the left wing → even more right yaw → increasingly uncoordinated flight. The correct understanding: adverse yaw is the price of aileron-induced lift differential. The correction is simultaneous left rudder with left aileron. The coordinated steep turn requires: left aileron + left rudder (to initiate) → maintain bank with slight back pressure → rudder to keep ball centered throughout. Uncoordinated steep turns with the ball displaced are a stall/spin risk factor. Option D is the 'complacency / let the plane fix itself' trap — adverse yaw does not self-correct without rudder input.
questions.sjt_rationale: This scenario tests whether the student has the conceptual foundation to diagnose an expected aerodynamic effect vs. a system malfunction. The hazardous escalation (more aileron to override apparent problem) is a Macho/Invulnerability response that makes the actual condition worse.

questions.text: During cruise at 5,500 feet, a pilot notices the elevator feels unusually stiff — requiring more force than normal to pitch the nose. A water bottle had been sitting on the avionics shelf. The pilot thinks: 'It's just temporary stiffness — maybe the trim is off. I'll try adjusting trim.' What is the safest course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Adjust elevator trim to compensate — if trim can relieve the stiffness, the flight may continue to destination; stiffness in the elevator is a normal variation between aircraft and does not indicate a control system problem

options.label: B
options.text: Suspect a physical obstruction in the elevator control linkage — the water bottle or other loose item may have migrated into the elevator control pushrod or bellcrank path; attempt to locate and remove the obstruction (check floor and seat tracks); if stiffness persists, reduce airspeed to decrease control forces, declare an emergency, and divert to the nearest suitable airport; do NOT rely on trim to compensate for mechanical restriction

options.label: C
options.text: Apply progressive back pressure to override the stiffness — if the elevator breaks free with sustained pressure, the restriction was temporary and flight may continue; if it does not break free with 40 lbs of force, then declare an emergency

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce power and descend slowly to the nearest airport — a power reduction will reduce airspeed and control loads making the stiff elevator more manageable; do not declare an emergency as ATC will create traffic conflicts; land and have the aircraft inspected

questions.explanation: Sudden restriction or unusual stiffness in a primary flight control is a potential emergency. Trim does not address mechanical restriction — it only relieves aerodynamic pressure on an otherwise freely-moving control. If the elevator control linkage has a physical obstruction, trim may provide temporary relief but the underlying restriction remains and could worsen (e.g., a loose item shifts further into the linkage path during descent or turbulence). The water bottle is a plausible cause — multiple NTSB reports document elevator and rudder restrictions from water bottles, maps, and other cabin items entering the control path under seats or along floor tracks. Correct actions: (1) Look for and remove the obstruction. (2) If stiffness persists or worsens, reduce airspeed to minimum control loads. (3) Declare emergency — ATC can provide vectoring to the nearest airport with immediate clearance. 'Applying progressive force to break it free' (Option C) risks causing physical damage to the control linkage if the obstruction is structural. Relying on trim (Option A) delays the diagnosis. Avoiding emergency declaration (Option D) deprives the pilot of ATC support precisely when they need it most.
questions.sjt_rationale: The 'it's probably just the trim' rationalization is Complacency combined with Invulnerability. The correct ADM chain: unusual primary control behavior → treat as potential emergency → investigate and reduce risk → get on the ground.
